positions/egalitarianism/oneLine: Men and women are equal not only in dignity but in authority and calling; ministry is determined by gifting rather than gender, and Christian marriage is a partnership of mutual submission.
positions/egalitarianism/coreClaims/0: Both male and female equally bear God’s image and receive the dominion mandate (Gen 1:26–28).
positions/egalitarianism/coreClaims/1: Patriarchal rule is a consequence of the fall (Gen 3:16), overcome in Christ (Gal 3:28).
positions/egalitarianism/coreClaims/2: Women served as prophets, deacons and apostles (Junia) in the New Testament.
positions/egalitarianism/coreClaims/3: Restrictive texts address specific situations, not a universal rule.
positions/egalitarianism/origin: Anticipated by Quaker women’s ministry (Margaret Fell, Women’s Speaking Justified, 1666), Methodist and Holiness women preachers (Phoebe Palmer, Catherine Booth), and early Pentecostal women; articulated in modern evangelicalism by Christians for Biblical Equality (1987; statement 1989); in mainline churches through women’s ordination from the 1950s–70s.
positions/egalitarianism/strongestArgume: The New Testament names women leaders (Phoebe, Priscilla, Junia) and prophesying women.
Pentecost’s outpouring on "sons and daughters" signals a new-creation equality.
The fruit of women’s ministry in revivals and missions (often a majority of missionaries) confirms God’s call.
positions/egalitarianism/strongestObject: Complementarians argue egalitarians reinterpret clear texts (1 Tim 2:12) by speculative reconstructions of background.
Catholic and Orthodox churches hold that the male priesthood reflects Christ’s maleness and the apostolic tradition.
Some argue egalitarian hermeneutics paved the way for revising sexual ethics.
positions/egalitarianism/responses/0: Egalitarians answer that interpreting texts in context is standard practice and is applied by complementarians too (e.g. head coverings).
positions/egalitarianism/responses/1: They distinguish the gender-roles question, grounded in Galatians 3:28 and New Testament practice, from sexual ethics, and many egalitarians hold the traditional sexual ethic.
positions/egalitarianism/consequences/0: Women’s ordination in most mainline and many Pentecostal and Wesleyan churches.
positions/egalitarianism/consequences/1: CBE International and egalitarian evangelical scholarship.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/altNa: Traditional view of marriage and sexuality
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/oneLi: Sexual intimacy is God’s gift for the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman; all sexual relations outside it, including same-sex sexual relations, fall short of God’s design, and those not married are called to chastity, supported by the church’s friendship and love.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/coreC: Creation establishes marriage as the union of male and female, reaffirmed by Jesus (Gen 1:27; 2:24; Matt 19:4–6).
Every biblical text that mentions same-sex intercourse prohibits it, in both Testaments (Lev 18:22; Rom 1:26–27; 1 Cor 6:9–11).
Sexual difference is integral to marriage’s symbolism of Christ and the Church (Eph 5:31–32).
Same-sex attraction is not itself sinful in most contemporary formulations; acting on it sexually is.
Christians with same-sex attraction are full members of the body of Christ, called with all unmarried believers to celibacy; churches must repent of contempt and hostility.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/origi: The consistent teaching of Jewish and early Christian moral catechesis (Didache 2; Clement of Alexandria; Chrysostom’s Homily 4 on Romans), medieval and Reformation theology; restated in modern documents such as the CDF’s Persona Humana (1975), the Catechism (1992, §§2357–2359), Lambeth I.10 (1998), the Nashville Statement (2017), and statements by Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox, evangelical and Pentecostal bodies.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/propo: Ecumenical Patriarchate and Russian Orthodox Church
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/stron: The witness of Scripture is uniform and grounds its sexual ethic in creation rather than only in cultural circumstances (Gagnon; Hays).
Jesus defined marriage by reference to "male and female" (Matt 19:4–5) and intensified, rather than relaxed, sexual ethics.
It is the unbroken consensus of the church across East and West for two millennia and of the great majority of Christians in the Global South today.
Ancient writers did know of mutual, adult same-sex relationships (e.g. in Plato’s Symposium), so the texts are not limited to exploitation.

Affirming scholars argue that the biblical writers had no concept of sexual orientation or of committed, egalitarian same-sex partnerships, so the texts do not address them (Brownson; Loader on context).

Requiring lifelong celibacy of all gay and lesbian people imposes a burden that Scripture elsewhere treats as a gift for some (1 Cor 7:7–9), and has been associated with documented harms to mental health.
The church once read Scripture to support slavery and the subordination of women; the experience of faithful LGBTQ Christians may likewise prompt re-reading (cf. Acts 15).
Historic teaching has been accompanied by contempt, criminalisation and violence that discredit it in the eyes of many.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/respo: Traditionalists reply that the creation-based structure of the argument (male and female) is unaffected by modern categories of orientation, and that Paul’s language in Romans 1 is general.
They answer that singleness and friendship should be honoured far more by churches, and that celibate gay Christians (e.g. Wesley Hill) testify to flourishing within the historic ethic.
They distinguish slavery, which Scripture regulates but never grounds in creation, from marriage, which it grounds in creation.

Many traditional churches have formally repented of hostility and oppose violence and criminalisation, while some Global South churches support criminal laws, a stance criticised by other traditionalists.
positions/traditional-sexual-ethic/conse: Official teaching of the large majority of the world’s churches.
GAFCON and realignment within Anglicanism; Global Methodist Church.
Debates over pastoral care, conversion therapy (widely rejected) and civil law.
positions/affirming-same-sex/oneLine: Faithful, lifelong, committed same-sex partnerships can embody the same covenant love, fidelity and mutual self-giving that Scripture honours in marriage; the church should bless and marry same-sex couples and fully include LGBTQ Christians in ministry.
positions/affirming-same-sex/coreClaims/: The handful of biblical prohibitions address forms of same-sex activity known in antiquity (pederasty, exploitation, excess of lust, cultic prostitution), not loving, committed partnerships between people of homosexual orientation.
The moral logic of marriage in Scripture is covenant faithfulness and one-flesh kinship (Brownson), which same-sex couples can share.
Mandatory celibacy for all gay people contradicts Scripture’s view of celibacy as a gift, not a requirement (1 Cor 7:7–9).
The fruit of the Spirit in LGBTQ Christians’ lives is evidence of God’s acceptance, as with Gentiles in Acts 10–15.
Justice, love of neighbour and the image of God require ending exclusion and discrimination.
positions/affirming-same-sex/keyTexts/0: Genesis 2:18 ("not good that the man should be alone")
positions/affirming-same-sex/keyTexts/4: 1 Samuel 18:1–3 (David and Jonathan, cited by some)
positions/affirming-same-sex/origin: Prepared by D. S. Bailey’s historical re-reading (1955), the Quaker report Towards a Quaker View of Sex (1963), the Metropolitan Community Church (1968) and John Boswell (1980); developed theologically by Eugene Rogers, James Alison, Dale Martin and James Brownson (2013), and popularised by Matthew Vines (God and the Gay Christian, 2014) and David Gushee (Changing Our Mind, 2014). Adopted by the United Church of Christ (2005), the Episcopal Church (2003–2015), ELCA (2009), PC(USA) (2014), Church of Scotland (2022), the Uniting Church in Australia (2018), the UMC (2024) and others.
positions/affirming-same-sex/strongestAr: Sexual orientation as a stable trait was unknown to the biblical writers; applying their prohibitions to it may be like applying ancient cosmology to modern astronomy.
Jesus’ ethic prioritises love, justice and the fruit of lives (Matt 7:16–20; 22:37–40), and the church has revised readings before (Gentile inclusion, slavery, usury, divorce).
The documented harm of exclusion — family rejection, depression and suicide among LGBTQ youth — is a moral concern the church cannot ignore.
Covenant fidelity, not sexual difference, is the moral centre of Scripture’s marriage teaching (Brownson).
positions/affirming-same-sex/strongestOb: Traditional scholars, including some who support civil equality, argue the biblical texts are clear and creation-based, and that ancient writers did know of consensual adult relationships (Gagnon; Hays; even some affirming scholars such as William Loader concede Paul would not have approved).
Jesus’ only definition of marriage refers to "male and female", and no biblical text affirms same-sex unions.
The view departs from the unanimous teaching of the church across two millennia and of the great majority of Christians today, especially in Africa and Asia, causing schism.
Experience and cultural change, critics argue, are being given authority over Scripture (a concern raised also about the Acts 15 analogy).
positions/affirming-same-sex/responses/0: Affirming theologians reply that Scripture itself models development under the Spirit (Acts 15), and that faithful readers now recognise contexts the writers did not envisage.
positions/affirming-same-sex/responses/1: They argue that the creation narrative emphasises companionship ("not good to be alone") more than complementarity, and that "male and female" describes the typical case without excluding others.
positions/affirming-same-sex/responses/2: They acknowledge the global disagreement and often call for structures (e.g. regional autonomy) that let churches differ without excommunication.
positions/affirming-same-sex/consequence: Same-sex marriage or blessing in many mainline Protestant and some Old Catholic churches.
Schisms and realignments (ACNA, GAFCON, Global Methodist Church, departures from ELCA and PC(USA)).
Ecumenical strain with Catholic, Orthodox and Global South churches.
positions/pro-life-abortion/oneLine: Human life is sacred from conception, so direct abortion is the unjust killing of an innocent human being; Christians should protect the unborn while supporting mothers and families.
positions/pro-life-abortion/coreClaims/0: Every human life bears God’s image from its beginning (Ps 139:13–16; Jer 1:5; Luke 1:41–44).
positions/pro-life-abortion/coreClaims/1: The early church condemned abortion and infanticide as murder (Didache 2; Athenagoras; Basil, canon 2).
positions/pro-life-abortion/coreClaims/2: Direct abortion is gravely wrong; many allow interventions to save the mother’s life (double effect) and differ on other exceptions.
positions/pro-life-abortion/coreClaims/3: A "consistent ethic of life" links opposition to abortion with concern for the poor, opposition to euthanasia and, for many, the death penalty.
positions/pro-life-abortion/coreClaims/4: Pro-life witness includes practical care for pregnant women and children.
positions/pro-life-abortion/origin: Continuous Christian teaching from the Didache (c.100) through Basil’s canons (c.375), medieval canon law (with debates about "ensoulment" timing) and the Reformers; reaffirmed by Vatican II (Gaudium et Spes 51), John Paul II’s Evangelium Vitae (1995), Orthodox bodies and evangelical leaders after Roe v. Wade (1973), notably Francis Schaeffer and C. Everett Koop (1979).
positions/pro-life-abortion/strongestArg: The unanimity of early Christian witness, in sharp contrast to pagan practice, shows abortion opposition is not a modern political invention.
Embryology confirms that a distinct human organism exists from conception.
Protecting the most vulnerable is central to biblical justice.
positions/pro-life-abortion/strongestObj: Pro-choice Christians argue that Scripture does not directly address abortion and that Exodus 21:22–25 may treat foetal loss differently from murder.
Medieval theologians (following Aristotle) held delayed ensoulment, so the moral status of early embryos was historically debated.
Critics say the movement has often focused on criminalisation over support for women and allied itself with partisan politics.
positions/pro-life-abortion/responses/0: Pro-life advocates answer that delayed-ensoulment theories still treated abortion as gravely sinful, and that modern biology removes the basis for them.
positions/pro-life-abortion/responses/1: Many emphasise crisis pregnancy support, adoption and social policy alongside legal protection.
positions/pro-life-abortion/consequences: Catholic–evangelical cooperation in the US pro-life movement.
Political influence culminating in Dobbs v. Jackson (2022) in the US.
